newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Europe fears Zaire will be worst-yet Africa crisis.
newsitem.headline: Europe fears Zaire will be worst-yet Africa crisis.

text.p: European politicians warned on Monday that a looming catastrophe in eastern Zaire could dwarf Africa's previous humanitarian tragedies, demanding a world response switching from apathy to action.
Zaire, whose leader Mobutu Sese Seko is in a private clinic in Switzerland after prostate cancer treatment, could be approaching a political "meltdown", they said.
"The end of Zaire has been predicted many times so I would urge caution," said one European Union diplomat.
"But the combination of factors this time round makes this potentially the most destabilising event Africa has ever seen."
All the familiar signs of a major African crisis fell into place on Monday, with hundreds of thousands of refugees on the move again.
And one shelter-area alone, eastern Zaire's Mugunga camp crowded with 420,000 homeless people, has become the world's biggest refugee camp.
Dishevelled aid workers have been trucked out, and disgruntled expatriates flown to safety.
"This could be the 'big one' -- the long-awaited Zairean melt-down," said one independent analyst.

What worries most Africa watchers is the overlapping and interlinked nature of the problems in Burundi, Rwanda, and eastern Zaire, and their potential to spill over into neighbouring states at the same time as a power vacuum in Zaire.

"A catastrophe greater than the one we knew in 1994 is what worries me most. I appeal to the combatants: please spare the refugees and local populations," Sadako Ogata, head of the U.N. refugee agency, UNHCR, said on Sunday.
Ogata was referring to the genocide in Rwanda when at least half a million people were slaughtered and the rivers of the Great Lakes region of central Africa were blocked with bloated bodies.

Ironically, it is that crisis that has partly created the current one. Ethnic conflicts in Burundi and Rwanda between Tutsis and Hutus, with separate historic and cultural roots, have essentially merged, spilling over into eastern Zaire, now home to refugees of ethnic groups from both countries.
They have become drawn into another feud between Zaireans and its own Banyamulenge Tutsi minority, motivated by vengeance and greed.

As so often in Africa, the crisis has been exacerbated by local politicians seeking to strengthen powerbases, distrust between regional leaders, and apathy in a West increasingly tired of the legacy of its colonial past.
Appeals for restraints are ignored. Meanwhile, the one man capable of exerting real influence in the area -- ailing Zairean President Mobutu -- remains off the political stage.

Diplomats and regional experts say the government is paralysed by the absence of a man whose mixed rule of brutality and guile has kept the huge, mineral-rich country together for more than three decades despite several secessionist movements.

Reports of his state of health are mixed. Whatever happens his corruption-ridden, near bankrupt government is unlikely to be able to restore order in the east, perhaps the trigger for the long-predicted post-Mobutu break-up of the anarchic country.

Prime Minister Kengo Wa Dondo, himself half-Tutsi, visited Brussels and London last week to press for international help -- a prospect viewed with horror in Brussels and Paris, the capitals of the countries most historically-linked to Zaire.

European Union diplomats, underlining their countries' failure to face up to the enormity of the potential crisis, have met only to discuss help for elections due next year as part of an EU-backed democratisation process.
Several provinces are already effectively autonomous and could remain unaffected by the events in the east.
